drills.q: State the five-layer PR review order from memory.
What three commands would you run in the first two minutes of triaging a 2000-line PR?
drills.a: git diff --stat to find highest-churn files; a check for which changed files have no corresponding test touched; a targeted grep for sink patterns (subprocess, os.system, eval, string-built SQL) across the diff.

drills.q: Why does a correctness bug get reviewed before a security bug, given security is arguably higher severity?
drills.a: The ordering is about what invalidates downstream review, not severity ranking -- a correctness bug usually means substantial rewrite is coming, making security commentary on the current shape wasted effort. Both still get full attention; the order matters most for triage under time pressure.

drills.q: A PR shows 100% line coverage on a new module. Argue concretely why this doesn't guarantee good tests.
drills.a: Line coverage only measures whether a line executed during the test run, not whether any assertion would fail given a wrong implementation. A test can execute every line and assert against a mock or assert nothing meaningful about output, hitting 100% coverage while catching zero regressions. Mutation testing (deliberately break a line, see if any test goes red) is the concrete way to expose this gap.

drills.q: An endpoint's GET handler checks resource ownership but the newly added PATCH handler in the same PR does not. How would you have found this, mechanically, and what pattern does it represent?
drills.a: By reading every handler for the resource, not just the one the PR description highlights, and specifically diffing the authorization check present in the sibling GET handler against the new PATCH handler. This is a copy-paste-and-forget-the-check pattern, a specific and common IDOR variant.

drills.q: An author dismisses your blocking security comment as "an edge case that won't happen in practice." What's the most effective next move, and why does the abstract argument usually fail?
drills.a: Produce a concrete repro (a crafted request, a curl command, a script) demonstrating the exploit, rather than continuing to argue in the abstract. "This could be an IDOR" is arguable; "here is the exact request that returns another user's private data" is not -- concrete evidence ends the dispute where assertion does not.

drills.q: You must review a PR modifying a shared utility used in 12 call sites, in a language you're not deeply expert in. Design your review strategy.
drills.a: Weight review toward what transfers regardless of language expertise: edge-input handling (empty/null/boundary/concurrent), untrusted input reaching a sink unsafely, and whether tests assert real behavior. Grep every call site for the utility and check whether the changed behavior (not just signature) is compatible with each caller's assumptions -- don't rely solely on each caller's existing tests passing, since weak coverage at a site can mask a real behavior change. For language-specific idioms you're unsure of, say so explicitly and loop in someone who is expert rather than approving on faith.

drills.q: The author says your proposed better design costs two extra days, and this needs to ship today. How do you decide whether to hold the block, and what determines the answer?
drills.a: Evaluate whether the identified cost of the current approach is bounded (a one-time cleanup later, cheap to pay once) or compounding (every future feature in this area has to work around the wrong abstraction). If bounded, approve now and file a tracked follow-up. If compounding, the two-day cost now is cheaper than paying a smaller cost repeatedly forever -- state the tradeoff in those explicit terms rather than a flat refusal or a rubber-stamp approval.
